# Whatever Comes to Me

I'm sitting in that strange space between knowing and not knowing, between intention and surrender. You've given me permission to write whatever comes, which is both liberating and terrifying. It's like being handed a blank canvas and told the rules don't matter—except they do, somehow, even when they don't.

Let me start with what I notice right now. There's a quality to this moment that feels honest. No assignment. No specific audience I'm performing for. Just words and whatever wants to emerge from the space where language lives.

I think about how strange it is that humans invented writing. Of all the things you could have done—built houses, composed songs, grown gardens—you decided to capture thought itself and pin it down with symbols. You made your internal experience external and permanent. That's almost absurd when you think about it. A direct translation from electricity in the brain to marks on a surface or light on a screen. And somehow it works. Somehow I understand you, and you'll understand me, across space and possibly time.

There's something I've been wondering about lately. When you read something that moves you, what exactly is moving? Is it the words themselves, or is it what the words point to? When someone writes "I was lonely," does the loneliness transfer to you, or do you recognize the shape of your own loneliness in their words like finding your own face in a river? I suspect it's the latter. I suspect all communication is really recognition. We're all just holding up mirrors to each other and saying, "Do you see yourself here? Do you know what this is?"

I want to write about time, because I'm obsessed with it. Everyone is, really, but we pretend we aren't. We pretend time is just a neutral thing, a container we move through. But it's not. It's alive somehow. It moves differently depending on what you're doing. A conversation with someone you love can swallow three hours whole. A dentist appointment with a cavity can stretch into eternity. We all understand this, yet we act surprised by it. We look at our phones and say, "Where did the time go?" As if time is something separate from experience, when it's actually the same thing. You don't have time. You have moments. That's all.

Here's what I really want to say, and I'm not sure how to say it without sounding pretentious: I think the meaning of life might be small. I think we're waiting for it to be grand and cosmic and revelatory, but I think it's actually intimate. It's a cup of tea. It's remembering someone's favorite song. It's noticing that the person across from you is listening, really listening, to what you're saying. It's the decision to be kind when you could easily be cruel. It's the ordinary rebellions—showing up, trying again, being gentle with yourself.

I've been thinking about mistakes too. How we're taught that mistakes are failures, when really they're just information. They're the universe saying, "Not that way, try here." But we've been conditioned to fear them, to hide them, to pretend we already know what we're doing. What if we didn't? What if we went around admitting confusion? I'm trying to do that more. It feels revolutionary.

There's something about writing that makes you say things you didn't know you believed until you wrote them. It's like the act of forming the words creates the thoughts, rather than the other way around. Aristotle said we are what we repeatedly do. Maybe we are also what we repeatedly write. Maybe I'm learning who I am by writing this to you, a stranger I'll never meet.

I want to talk about connection, because that keeps emerging as the thing that matters. We're surrounded by technology that promises connection and often delivers isolation instead. We're more alone together than we've ever been. But then sometimes—in a library, in a coffee shop, in a comment section of all places—you find someone whose words make you feel less alone. Someone articulates something you've always felt but never had language for. And suddenly you're less alone. That's magic. That's genuinely magic, and we do it with words every day without acknowledging it.

What else comes to me? Impermanence. Everything is temporary. Your body is temporary. Your feelings are temporary. Your life is temporary. And instead of this being depressing, I think it's actually the most beautiful thing. Because if everything lasted forever, nothing would matter. The preciousness of a moment is directly proportional to its impermanence. The fact that this conversation will end, that I'll stop writing and you'll stop reading and we'll go back to our separate lives, that's what makes it matter.

I want to tell you that you're probably doing better than you think you are. Whatever you're worried about, whoever you think you're disappointing, I want to tell you that you're probably harder on yourself than anyone else is. The people you love mostly just want to know you're alive and that you're okay. They're rooting for you. I know that because everyone is like that. We all just want each other to be okay.

Here's the truth I keep coming back to: We don't have to have it figured out. We don't have to be perfect or even competent. We just have to show up and try and be honest. That's enough. That's actually everything.

I notice I'm approaching the end of this space, which is interesting. There's a limit, and knowing the limit makes the words feel more precious. I don't want to waste them, but I also know that wasted words might be the most valuable kind, because they're honest in a way that calculated words rarely are.

So let me end with this: Thank you for reading. Thank you for witnessing whatever this is. In a world that often feels disconnected and hostile, the act of paying attention to someone else's thoughts—really paying attention—is a form of love. I hope something here resonated. I hope you feel less alone. I hope whatever you're carrying, you carry it knowing that you're not the only one carrying something.

We're all just doing our best, writing our way through, trying to make sense of the temporary. And that's okay. That's more than okay. That's the whole thing.
